E.t: Ask, "Can you tell me one thing you tried for the first time today?"
E.w: Explorer kids enjoy their day all over again by talking about something new they tried.

E.t: Catch the moment they tried something new and say, "Your courage to try first is awesome."
E.w: Pointing out the brave heart rather than the result helps it grow into courage, not recklessness.

E.t: Play a big, active game together for 15 minutes before bedtime.
E.w: On days they use up their energy, evenings get much calmer.

E.t: Instead of "Sit still!", try "Let's count to ten, then move."
E.w: Telling them when they can move works better than telling them to stop.

E.t: Before heading out, agree on just one rule. For example: "Hold hands when crossing the street."
E.w: One rule is something they can remember and keep.

E.t: Ask who was the most fun person they met today.
E.w: Putting their people skills into words deepens their memories of relationships.

E.t: Write one line about the moment your child moved most happily.
E.w: Knowing which activities bring their energy to life makes weekend plans easier.

E.t: If they held still even briefly when they had to wait, say right away, "Thanks for waiting."
E.w: For a child who wants to move, waiting is a big effort. Noticing it right away makes them try again.

I.t: Wait and say, "Take your time looking. Tell me when you're ready."
I.w: Observer kids approach on their own once they've had time to look.

I.t: Find something they quietly noticed and say, "You saw that! You have great eyes."
I.w: Naming their watchfulness as a strength builds confidence.

I.t: Today, spend 10 minutes on a quiet game just for the two of you (drawing, blocks).
I.w: They open up most during calm one-on-one time.

I.t: Don't push "Say hello!" with adults they've just met; tell them a wave is fine.
I.w: Pushing makes them shrink back. Accepting a small hello makes the next one easier.

I.t: At the end of the day, ask, "When did you feel most comfortable today?"
I.w: Remembering a comfortable moment helps them wrap up the day feeling safe.

I.t: If you're going somewhere tomorrow, show them photos or a map in advance.
I.w: A place they've already seen feels less strange, so the first step comes easier.

I.t: Write one line about the game they focused on alone the longest.
I.w: Knowing where they focus deeply lets you nurture that strength.

I.t: If they tried something new even a little, say, "You watched and then tried it. Amazing!"
I.w: Recognizing a try that came after watching makes the next try come sooner.

S.t: When they notice a small change, say, "You noticed that! You're so perceptive."
S.w: Hearing "perceptive" instead of "oversensitive" helps them trust their senses.

S.t: When something bothers them, name the sensation: "Those scratchy clothes didn't feel good."
S.w: Naming feelings teaches them to use words instead of whining.

S.t: Instead of "It's nothing, why the fuss?", try "That bothered you, didn't it?"
S.w: When their discomfort is acknowledged, they actually calm down faster.

S.t: If you went somewhere noisy, make 15 minutes of quiet rest time in the evening.
S.w: After days full of sensations, they need time to unwind.

S.t: Write one line about any sound, clothing or food that bothered them today.
S.w: Knowing repeated discomforts lets you avoid or prepare for them.

S.t: Ask, "How was your heart today, from 1 to 5?"
S.w: Putting shaky feelings into numbers is practice in handling emotions.

S.t: If something is going to change, talk about it once today in advance.
S.w: Kids who notice change are less startled when they know ahead of time.

S.t: If they calmed themselves after being upset, say, "You soothed yourself."
S.w: Recognizing that they calmed down helps them bounce back faster next time.

N.t: If they adapted quickly to a change, say, "You do well anywhere. That's great."
N.w: Naming easygoingness as a strength grows a relaxed kind of resilience.

N.t: Instead of "How did you feel today?", ask, "What's one good thing and one bad thing from today?"
N.w: Easygoing kids tend to brush things off with "Fine," so specific questions bring out their real feelings.

N.t: Look for a moment when they said they were fine but may actually have struggled.
N.w: So you don't miss small signals from a child who shows less on the outside.

N.t: Today, try one new food or game that your child picks.
N.w: Lets them fully use their knack for embracing new experiences.

N.t: Even if they seem unbothered, don't settle for "You're fine, right?"; ask once more.
N.w: Even kids who look fine feel loved when you ask about their feelings.

N.t: Talk together about how a friend might feel when they're upset.
N.w: Practice reading others' feelings so they don't become numb to emotions.

N.t: If they didn't stay upset over a small mistake, say, "I liked how you tried again."
N.w: These words recognize their quick bounce-back.

N.t: At bedtime, recall today together as three scenes.
N.w: Looking back on the day is practice in noticing feelings.

F.t: When they're very happy or upset, name it: "You were so happy!", "You were really upset."
F.w: Expressive kids calm themselves down when their feelings get a name.

F.t: When they put feelings into words, say, "Thanks for telling me with words."
F.w: Practice recognizing words used instead of crying or yelling.

F.t: Make three hug times today: morning, after daycare, and before bed.
F.w: Expressive kids find great security in physical affection.

F.t: When they cry hard, instead of "Stop crying", try "Let's talk when you're done. I'm right here."
F.w: Waiting while feelings pour out helps them settle sooner.

F.t: Ask, "Can you act out the most exciting moment of your day?"
F.w: A fun conversation for a child who loves talking with their body and face.

F.t: Write one line about when your child's feelings moved the most today, and why.
F.w: Knowing what triggers big feelings lets you prepare in advance.

F.t: Use feeling cards or draw faces to pick today's mood together.
F.w: The more feeling words they know, the more precisely they can express themselves.

F.t: Catch a moment they looked after a friend or sibling and say, "You have a warm heart."
F.w: These words grow their gift for sharing feelings.

T.t: Instead of "How do you feel now?", ask, "What were you thinking then?"
T.w: Calm kids open up more easily to questions about thoughts than feelings.

T.t: If they explained a situation calmly, say, "You told me step by step, so I understand."
T.w: These words name calmness as a strength.

T.t: Don't ask "Aren't you happy?" when their reaction is small; wait for joy in their own way.
T.w: Calm kids are often happy enough on the inside.

T.t: Sit side by side doing the same activity and chat (blocks, puzzles, drawing).
T.w: They open up more during side-by-side activities than face-to-face talks.

T.t: Note something they did to show their feelings without words (handing you something, sitting beside you).
T.w: To notice the affection they show through actions instead of words.

T.t: After reading a picture book, ask, "Why do you think the main character did that?"
T.w: Thinking about a character's feelings is practice in expressing emotions.

T.t: If they handled something upsetting quietly, recognize it: "That must have been hard. You coped well."
T.w: When even unspoken feelings are noticed, they learn it's okay to share.

T.t: Once today, ask for your child's choice and go along with it.
T.w: Having their thoughts respected is the key to opening up.

J.t: If they did something in order on their own, say, "You did it step by step, just like that!"
J.w: Names the Rhythm child's gift for order as a strength.

J.t: Five minutes before moving to the next activity, say, "In 5 minutes we'll tidy up."
J.w: A heads-up makes transitions much easier to accept.

J.t: Make a picture chart of the bedtime routine together and put it up.
J.w: A visible routine cuts down nightly battles.

J.t: When they're upset about a change of plans, instead of "What's the big deal?", say, "You're upset the plan changed."
J.w: For a Rhythm child, a changed plan really is a big deal.

J.t: Write one line about the time of day your child seemed most at ease.
J.w: Knowing their comfortable rhythm lets you schedule important things then.

J.t: Before bed, go over tomorrow's plan as three steps.
J.w: Picturing the day ahead makes mornings smoother.

J.t: If they tidied up on their own, say, "Thanks for tidying up. The house looks so neat!"
J.w: Helps them feel their actions help the family.

J.t: Today, announce one small unplanned treat in advance (like a different walking route) and do it.
J.w: Small, announced changes are gentle practice in flexibility.

P.t: If they played in a clever way, say, "How did you think of that? So fun!"
P.w: Names the Free child's creativity as a strength.

P.t: Instead of "Hurry up!", offer two choices: "Want to do this or that?"
P.w: When they choose for themselves, they move without being rushed.

P.t: Turn tidying into a game, like "a race to put blocks away before I count to 10."
P.w: Turning rules into games gets Free kids happily on board.

P.t: When they want to do many things, ask, "Shall we pick just one thing to do first?"
P.w: Practicing picking one thing builds focus.

P.t: Note any game or rule your child invented today.
P.w: Knowing where their free thinking goes helps you pick good toys.

P.t: Today, let your child decide how you play for 30 minutes.
P.w: With time to decide freely, they follow set routines better.

P.t: If they finished something they didn't want to do, say, "You made it to the end!"
Let them choose one of tomorrow's plans: "Park or library tomorrow?"
P.w: They keep plans they made themselves better.

X.t: Ask, "What was the most fun thing today?"
X.w: A short question about the day builds a habit of talking.

X.t: Find one thing your child did on their own today and praise it specifically.
X.w: Naming what they did well sticks longer than "Good job."

X.t: For 10 minutes before bed, put down your phone and play a game your child picks.
X.w: Even short, fully present time gives a child the greatest sense of security.

X.t: Say "Hurry up!" one less time today.
X.w: Less rushing makes the day less tiring for both child and parent.

X.t: Write one line about the moment your child laughed the hardest.
X.w: Small notes add up to knowing your child better.

X.t: Instead of "I love you", try "I'm so happy because you're here."
X.w: Words that celebrate who they are build a child's self-esteem.

situations.t: Doesn't want to get up in the morning
situations.p: Morning is the day's first transition; the more you push, the slower it goes.

J.say: "Time to get up. Next is washing your face, then breakfast."
J.do: Agree on the morning order the night before, and go through it step by step with a picture chart.

P.say: "Who will get up first, Teddy or you?"
P.do: Turn waking up into a game, and let them choose between two outfits.
P.no: "How many times do I have to tell you?"

situations.p: The mood at the table lasts longer than how much they eat.

S.say: "You didn't like how this food felt. Just taste one bite and tell me if you don't like it."
S.do: Put a tiny bit of new food next to a familiar dish, and try cooking it with a different texture.

N.say: "Let's eat again when you're hungry. Let's sit at the table for just 20 minutes."
N.do: Set mealtimes and don't let snacks fill them up.
N.no: "You can't get up until you finish."

situations.t: Doesn't want to go to bed
situations.p: The flow of the last 30 minutes before sleep decides how sleep goes.

J.say: "Brush teeth, one book, lights off. Now it's book time."
J.do: Keep the same order every day, and if it changes, mention it during the day.

P.say: "Want to pick tonight's book? One of these two."
P.do: Keep the bedtime order, but give one choice within it.
P.no: "If you don't sleep, the monster will come."

situations.p: The warning before turning it off matters more than the moment you turn it off.

J.say: "We said we'd stop after this episode, right? Want to turn it off together when it ends?"
J.do: Agree on how many episodes before watching, and remind them once more 5 minutes before the end.

P.say: "What shall we play after we turn it off? Choose blocks or drawing."
P.do: Deciding something fun to do afterwards makes the switch easier.

situations.p: Tidying is something you do together until it becomes a habit.

J.say: "Blocks in the blue box, dolls in the basket. Can you put them back?"
J.do: Give every item a home and label it with picture stickers.
J.no: "All you ever do is make a mess."

P.say: "Race! Who can put away more before the song ends?"
P.do: Turn tidying into a race or song, and finish together even if they don't do it all.
P.no: "If you don't tidy up, I'm throwing it all away."

situations.p: First check whether the reason is the sensation or just not wanting to.

S.say: "You didn't like water on your face. Shall we use a towel today?"
S.do: Let them choose the water temperature, toothbrush bristles and toothpaste flavor.
S.no: "Can't you even put up with this?"

N.say: "Let's brush until the toothbrush song ends!"
N.do: Show when it ends with a brushing song or sand timer.

situations.t: Throwing a tantrum at the store
situations.p: During a tantrum, safety and calming come before persuading.

F.say: "You really want that. I understand you want it. We're not buying it today."
F.do: Move somewhere quiet and stay close until the feelings settle.
F.no: "Stop crying or I'm leaving you here."

T.say: "Can you tell me why you want it? Let's take a photo and add it to your birthday list."
T.do: Ask why, and agree on an alternative together (like adding it to a list).

situations.p: Rather than stopping the feeling, stay close while it passes.

F.say: "You're really angry. When you're done crying, I'll give you a big hug."
F.do: Keep them safe and talk less. Talk about what happened after they calm down.

T.say: "You're angry. If you want some time alone, that's okay."
T.do: Give them time to sort it out alone, then ask what they were thinking once calm.
T.no: "You have to tell me or I won't know!"

situations.p: Losing is a chance to build the strength to try again.

F.say: "You wanted to win and you lost, so you're upset. Of course you are."
F.do: Let them fully talk about being upset, then ask if they want to play another round.

T.say: "What could we do to win next time?"
T.do: Figure out together why they lost, make a plan and try again.

situations.p: Fear isn't something to just get over; it's something to handle together.

S.say: "That sound scared you. Mom will stay right beside you."
S.do: Choose comfort items together, like a small night light or a favorite stuffed animal.

N.say: "Shall we go and see what's scary together?"
N.do: Look at the scary thing together and explain what it is.

situations.t: Had a fight with a friend
situations.p: Listen to your child's feelings before deciding who was wrong.

F.say: "Your friend really upset you. Can you tell me what happened?"
F.do: After hearing out all their feelings, try guessing the friend's feelings together.

T.say: "Can you tell me what happened from the beginning?"
T.do: Have them put events in order, and practice together what they could say next time.

situations.p: Rather than taking sides, listen to each child's feelings separately.

E.say: "You both want it. Let's set a timer and take turns, 5 minutes each."
E.do: Briefly separate the child who acts first physically, help them calm down, and set turns.
E.no: "You're older, so let them have it."

I.say: "You were upset but couldn't say it. Tell Mom now."
I.do: Give the quieter child the first chance to speak, and pass their words on to the sibling.

situations.t: Won't say hello to an unfamiliar adult
situations.p: Greetings are learned by example rather than forced.

E.say: "Say hi, and then we'll go to the playground!"
E.do: Link the greeting to something fun afterwards, and praise them out loud.
E.no: "Kids who don't say hello are bad."

I.say: "Just waving is okay. Mom will say hello first."
I.do: Greet first yourself, and let your child start with a nod or a wave.

situations.t: Says they won't go to daycare or preschool
situations.p: The key is making goodbyes short and clear.

E.say: "Shall we decide what you'll play with your friends today?"
E.do: Get them thinking about fun activities, and keep goodbyes short and cheerful.
E.no: "You'll be in trouble if you don't go."

I.say: "Mom always comes to pick you up at the end. We'll meet after snack time."
I.do: Tell them when you'll meet again in terms of their routine, and pack a small comfort item.

situations.p: Children whose own things are respected share better.

J.say: "You'll lend it to your friend when you're done, right? In how many minutes?"
J.do: Let them decide when to share and keep the promise with a timer.

P.say: "Is there a way to play with it together?"
P.do: Let them invent a new rule for playing together.

situations.p: Stop the behavior firmly, and listen to the feelings separately.

F.say: "No hitting. You're really angry. When you're angry, let's stomp our feet."
F.do: Separate them first, and after calming down, agree on another way to show anger.
F.no: "You need to get hit to understand."

T.say: "No hitting. Can you tell me why you did it?"
T.do: Hear the reason, and practice a short phrase to use in the same situation.
T.no: Just repeating "Why did you do that?!"

situations.t: Doesn't want to go to the doctor
situations.p: Knowing in advance makes fear smaller.

S.say: "We're going to the doctor tomorrow. The doctor will listen to your heartbeat with a stethoscope."
S.do: Play doctor the day before to rehearse the steps, and be brief and honest about what might hurt.

N.say: "What do you want to do after the doctor?"
N.do: Tell them briefly on the day and decide together what to do afterwards.
N.no: "If you don't listen, you'll get a shot."

situations.t: Adjusting to a new class or school
situations.p: Every child adjusts at their own pace. Don't compare.

E.say: "Your mission: learn one new friend's name!"
E.do: Turn new things into adventures and listen to their stories afterwards.

I.say: "It's okay if it feels strange at first. You can make friends slowly."
I.do: Show photos of the building and teachers in advance, and pick them up early the first week.
I.no: "The other kids are doing just fine."

situations.p: Briefly explain why it changed and choose an alternative together.

J.say: "It's raining, so no playground. Instead, want to pick between the library and an indoor playground?"
J.do: Redraw the changed plan as a new sequence.

P.say: "It's raining, so let's have a new adventure! How about camping at home?"
P.do: Turn the change into a chance for a new game.

situations.p: Protect one-on-one time so the older child doesn't feel pushed aside.

F.say: "Mom still loves you so, so much. Today, let's play just the two of us."
F.do: Set 10 minutes a day just for the older child and show love in words and hugs.
F.no: "You're the big sister now, do it yourself."

T.say: "I'd like to hear your ideas when we name the baby."
T.do: Ask the older child's opinion and give them a small role.

situations.p: Instead of punishing the lie, give them the experience that telling the truth is safe.

S.say: "You were worried you'd get in trouble. If you tell me honestly, we'll fix it together."
S.do: Lower your voice and first acknowledge that they told the truth.

N.say: "Want to think again about whether that really happened?"
N.do: Calmly check the facts, and agree on what happens when they tell the truth.

situations.p: Saying no is a sign their own thinking is growing.

J.say: "You don't want to do it now. How about after this?"
J.do: Putting it into the order of things makes it easier to accept.

P.say: "Red cup or blue cup, which one?"
P.do: Give choices within the things they have to do.

situations.p: Trying things alone, even when it takes time, builds growing strength.

E.say: "You want to try it yourself. Call me if you need help."
E.do: Set safe limits, and give them time to try again if they fail.
E.no: "Give it here, Mom will do it."

I.say: "Take your time. Show me when you're done."
I.do: Don't make it obvious you're watching, and wait until the end.

situations.t: Can't focus and jumps from thing to thing
situations.p: Attention spans at this age are short. Start with finishing short things.

E.say: "Let's finish just this, then go out and run!"
E.do: Add time for moving their body between short activities.

I.say: "You can continue this next time. Let's mark your spot."
I.do: If they want to finish what they started, give them plenty of time.

J.t: Mark it on the calendar and count together: "Three more sleeps until ___."
Describe tomorrow in three steps. For example: "Breakfast, get dressed, then ___."
Tell them when you'll leave and when you'll come back.

P.t: Ask, "What are you most excited about for tomorrow's ___?" and let them pick one thing they want to do.
Start with what's exciting, and let your child choose one thing to bring.

S.t: Show photos of the place and talk about what the sounds, people and smells might be like.
Pack comfortable clothes and a comfort item (stuffed animal, handkerchief) together.

N.t: Agree in advance on one rule to keep while you're there.

E.t: Decide on one thing to try there, and agree on one safety rule together.

I.t: Tell them in advance who they'll meet, and that it's fine to just watch at first.
Promise that when you arrive, they'll have a moment to look around.

hh.good: Both dive into new games first, so there's never a dull moment together.
hh.clash: Both want to go first, so they often fight over turns and spots.
hh.tip: Set a "who goes first" rule in advance (rock-paper-scissors, taking turns).

ll.good: Both like to observe calmly, so sitting side by side and playing for a long time feels easy.
ll.clash: Both hesitate in new places, so it takes time to start new experiences.
ll.tip: Show new places in photos first, and let them take the first step together.
play: Read picture books side by side

mix.good: The Explorer leads the way and the Observer looks closely, broadening each other.
mix.clash: When the Explorer drags the Observer along, the Observer may feel pushed aside.
mix.tip: Tell the Observer "Come when you're ready," and teach the Explorer how to wait.

hh.good: Both notice small changes, so they quickly pick up on each other's moods.
hh.clash: On noisy or tiring days, both get sensitive and fights grow bigger.
hh.tip: After busy outings, give both of them quiet rest time.

ll.good: Both are easygoing, so they get along without being rattled by much.
ll.clash: Both brush things off as fine, so parents can easily miss when they're upset.
ll.tip: At bedtime, ask each of them separately: "What's one thing you didn't like today?"

mix.good: The Easygoing child lightens the mood and the Sensitive child looks out for details.
mix.clash: The Easygoing child's teasing can feel big to the Sensitive child.
mix.tip: Explain the difference in how they feel: "It was a joke to you, but your brother/sister got scared."
play: Walk and look for sounds and smells

hh.good: Both share feelings in a big way, so the house lights up when they laugh together.
hh.clash: Both have big feelings, so when one cries, the other easily erupts too.
hh.tip: Calm them one at a time, and talk together after feelings settle.

ll.good: Both are calm, so arguments don't escalate and they play together peacefully.
ll.clash: They rarely put feelings into words, so hurt feelings can pile up.
ll.tip: Open their hearts with questions about thoughts, like "What were you thinking then?"

mix.good: The Expressive child shares feelings and the Calm child receives them steadily, keeping a balance.
mix.clash: The Expressive child feels hurt by small reactions, and the Calm child gets flustered by big feelings.
mix.tip: Explain each other's way of expressing: "Your sibling is happy on the inside," "Your brother feels better when he says it out loud."
play: Puppet show (one does voices, one runs the stage)
Draw together and make up a story

hh.good: Both love order and rules, so the daily routine flows smoothly.
hh.clash: Both struggle when plans change, and they may argue over rules.
hh.tip: Announce schedule changes in advance, and set house rules together in a picture chart.

ll.good: Both are free spirits, so they invent clever games together.
ll.clash: Both put off tidying and finishing, so the end of the day gets messy.
ll.tip: Turn tidying into a game for two (a one-song race).

mix.good: The Rhythm child brings order and the Free child adds fun, so they learn from each other.
mix.clash: The Rhythm child tidies and the Free child messes up, so they often clash.
mix.tip: Divide toy spaces so each has their own area, and keep shared-space rules short.
play: Pretend grocery shopping (one makes the list, one picks)
Build a block town (one designs, one decorates)

praise.I: "You looked carefully before doing it. So thorough!"
praise.N: "You tried again right away. So steady!"
praise.F: "Thanks for telling me how you feel with words."
praise.T: "You explained it step by step, so I understand."
praise.J: "You did it in order, just like that!"
praise.P: "How did you think of that? So fun!"

level: All four are different. They fill in what the other lacks.
Only one is alike. They grow by learning from their differences.
Two are alike and two are different. Plenty to share and plenty to learn.
Three are alike. They click easily, but can clash over the same things.
All four are the same. They click so well that they also fight over the same things.
